card.title: EMF, Internal Resistance and Cells in Combination

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **EMF ($\mathcal{E}$):** the open-circuit voltage of a source. It is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
**EMF vs Terminal Voltage:** EMF ($\mathcal{E}$) is the open-circuit voltage (no current). Terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ under discharge; $V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$ during charging.…
**Series/Parallel Cell Rules:** In series: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \sum \mathcal{E}_i$, $r_{total} = \sum r_i$. In parallel (identical cells): $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}$, $r_{total} = r/n$.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Maximum Power Transfer Theorem:** Maximum power to load $R$ occurs at $R = r$, giving $P_{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$. At this point, efficiency is 50%. For efficiency $>50\%$, need $R > r$; for $>90\%$, need $R > 9r$.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The internal resistance of a typical AA alkaline cell is about 0.15 $\\\Omega$ when fresh, but increases to 0.5 $\\\Omega$ or more as it discharges.  ·  Connecting cells in series increases the available voltage while keeping the same current capacity. Connecting in parallel increases the current capacity while keeping the same voltage.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 $\\\Omega$ is connected to a 7 $\\\Omega$ resistor. Find the current, terminal voltage, and power delivered to the resistor. Solution: $I = 1.5/(7+0.5) = 0.2$ A. $V = 1.5 - 0.2 \ imes 0.5 = 1.4$ V. $P = I^2 R = 0.04 \ imes 7 = 0.28$ W.  ·  A cell gives 2.0 V when no current flows and 1.8 V when delivering 1 A. Find the EMF and internal resistance. Solution: EMF $\mathcal{E} = 2.0$ V (open circuit). Under load: $1.8 = 2.0 - 1 \ imes r$, so $r = 0.2\\\\,$\Omega$.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: EMF is not a force - it is a voltage (energy per unit charge). The name is historical. EMF is measured in volts, not newtons.  ·  Terminal voltage $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$ is less than EMF when current flows out of the cell. But when charging the cell, current flows into the positive terminal, so $V = \\\\mathcal{E} + Ir$ - the terminal voltage is greater than EMF.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Internal resistance $r$:** the resistance inside the cell due to electrolyte and electrodes. It causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows.  ·  **Terminal voltage:** $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$. When no current flows ($I=0$), $V = \mathcal{E}$. Under load, $V < \mathcal{E}$.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: A short-circuited 12 V car battery with internal resistance 0.01 $\\\Omega$ can deliver 1200 A, which is why it can melt tools and cause severe burns.  ·  The maximum power transfer theorem ($R = r$) is a fundamental design principle for matching loads to sources, but it is inefficient for power distribution systems where $R \\\\gg r$ is desired.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Three identical cells of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.3 $\\\Omega$ each are connected in series across a 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = 4.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.9\\\\,$\Omega$. $I = 4.5/(6+0.9) = 0.652$ A.  ·  The same three cells above are connected in parallel across the same 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = 1.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.3/3 = 0.1\\\\,$\Omega$. $I = 1.5/(6+0.1) = 0.246$ A.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: In series, both EMF and internal resistance add. In parallel, the equivalent EMF is the same as one cell, but the equivalent internal resistance is reduced, allowing more current.  ·  Maximum power transfer ($R = r$) occurs at 50% efficiency. For efficient power delivery, you want $R \\\\gg r$ (high efficiency, low power). For maximum power, you sacrifice efficiency.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: In a battery pack, series strings are often used to increase voltage, and parallel strings within each series group are used to increase capacity and reduce internal resistance.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Cells in series:** $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}_1 + \mathcal{E}_2 + \ldots$, $r_{total} = r_1 + r_2 + \ldots$. Series adds both EMF and internal resistance.  ·  **Cells in parallel:** $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}$ (if all equal), $r_{total} = r/n$ for $n$ identical cells. Parallel reduces internal resistance, allowing higher current delivery.  ·  **Maximum power transfer:** the power delivered to an external load $R$ is maximum when $R = r$. The maximum power is $P_{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A fresh battery has a high open-circuit voltage (close to its EMF) but drops significantly under load if its internal resistance has increased with age. That is why old batteries seem weak.  ·  Find the external resistance for maximum power transfer to a cell with EMF 12 V and internal resistance 2 $\\\Omega$. Find the maximum power. Solution: $R = r = 2\\\\,$\Omega$. $I = 12/(2+2) = 3$ A. $P_{max} = I^2 R = 9 \ imes 2 = 18$ W. Alternatively $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r) = 144/8 = 18$ W.  ·  **Current in a simple circuit:** $I = \mathcal{E}/(R + r)$, where $R$ is the external resistance and $r$ is the internal resistance.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Efficiency:** the efficiency of power transfer is $\eta = R/(R + r)$. Maximum efficiency approaches 100% when $R \gg r$, but maximum power requires $R = r$.  ·  **Short circuit current:** when $R = 0$, $I_{sc} = \\\\mathcal{E}/r$. This can be very large and dangerous, causing heating and damage.  ·  **Cells with different EMFs:** when cells with different EMFs are connected in parallel, circulating currents flow between them. This can damage cells and should be avoided.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Real cell behavior:** as a cell discharges, its EMF slowly decreases and its internal resistance increases. An old battery reads lower than its rated voltage even when not loaded.
